articles.title: Hytalo Santos: Justiça da Paraíba nega recurso e mantém influenciador preso | G1
articles.standfirst: Câmara Criminal do TJPB analisou nesta terça-feira (3) pedido de soltura de Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente. Defesa buscava revogar prisão preventiva.
articles.summary: Câmara Criminal do TJPB analisou nesta terça-feira (3) pedido de soltura de Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente. Defesa buscava revogar prisão preventiva.
articles.body:
Hytalo Santos vai ser solto? Tribunal de Justiça analisa recurso que pode tirar influenciador da cadeia na Paraíba — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A Câmara Criminal do Tribunal de Justiça da Paraíba (TJPB) negou, nesta terça-feira (3), o recurso da defesa de Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente que pedia a revogação da prisão preventiva. Com a decisão, os dois permanecem presos no Presídio Desembargador Flóscolo da Nóbrega, em João Pessoa .

O julgamento foi realizado de forma semipresencial. O recurso analisado trata da prisão preventiva do influenciador e do marido, que foram condenados em fevereiro de 2026 por produção de conteúdo pornográfico envolvendo adolescentes.

A defesa buscava a soltura dos dois. No entanto, a decisão da Câmara Criminal mantém a situação de prisão preventiva.

Hytalo Santos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A investigação sobre Hytalo Santos começou antes da repercussão nacional do caso. Em 17 de dezembro de 2024, o Ministério Público da Paraíba (MPPB) informou que apurava denúncias relacionadas à possível exploração de crianças e adolescentes em conteúdos publicados nas redes sociais.

Natural de Cajazeiras, Hytalo tinha, na época, 16,9 milhões de seguidores em um dos perfis nas redes sociais. Segundo o MPPB, as investigações buscavam esclarecer a participação de menores de idade nas produções feitas pelo influenciador.

À época das suspeitas, o influenciador publicou vídeos nas próprias redes sociais se defendendo e alegando que existia uma relação com o que ele chamou de "crias", que são os adolescentes que frequentam a casa dele. Disse ainda que a assessoria jurídica tratava da questão e que sempre que surgia uma denúncia os fatos eram rapidamente esclarecidos.

Vídeo de Felca amplia repercussão do caso

Felca é Youtuber e influenciador; Ele denunciou Hytalo Santos — Foto: Youtube

Entre os exemplos apresentados, Felca mencionou a participação de Kamyla Santos, à época com 17 anos, e afirmou que a imagem da jovem era explorada de forma sensual para gerar audiência e lucro nas redes sociais. O youtuber também exibiu trechos de vídeos publicados por Hytalo e criticou o tipo de conteúdo produzido.

Em um dos momentos do vídeo, Felca afirmou:

“Qual a problemática maior aqui, além deles serem adolescentes, não estarem com o lobo pré-frontal desenvolvido e não terem a mínima ideia do que é um relacionamento e as consequências de suas ações [...]".

Dois dias depois, em 8 de agosto, a conta de Hytalo Santos deixou de ficar disponível no Instagram.

Justiça bloqueia redes sociais e proíbe contato com adolescentes

Em 12 de agosto de 2025, a Justiça da Paraíba determinou o bloqueio do acesso de Hytalo Santos às redes sociais e proibiu o influenciador de ter contato com os adolescentes citados no processo.

A decisão também determinou a desmonetização dos conteúdos publicados por Hytalo. O pedido havia sido feito pelo Ministério Público da Paraíba em uma ação civil pública.

O MP informou ao g1 que Hytalo foi ouvido em um dos procedimentos no dia 30 de maio de 2025, em Bayeux. Segundo o órgão, os adolescentes não foram ouvidos novamente para evitar revitimização, já que já tinham prestado depoimento em outro processo.

O promotor João Arlindo afirmou que Hytalo também foi ouvido em outro braço da investigação e negou as acusações.

As plataformas também adotaram medidas. O Google informou que já havia desmonetizado o canal e retirado conteúdos que violavam diretrizes. O TikTok informou que um perfil do influenciador foi banido pela segunda vez em 2025. Já a conta de Kamyla Santos foi desativada, segundo a Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas do Ministério da Fazenda, por publicidade de apostas feita por menor de idade.

Busca e apreensão mirou aparelhos eletrônicos

No dia 13 de agosto de 2025, a Polícia cumpriu mandado de busca e apreensão na residência de Hytalo Santos, em um condomínio no bairro Portal do Sol, em João Pessoa.

Hytalo não foi encontrado no local. Segundo informações registradas no cumprimento do mandado, funcionários do condomínio relataram que o influenciador havia saído antes da chegada das equipes levando equipamentos em um veículo.

No dia seguinte, em 14 de agosto de 2025, a Justiça da Paraíba autorizou um novo pedido de busca e apreensão em três endereços ligados a Hytalo Santos, todos em João Pessoa.

As buscas foram autorizadas na residência do influenciador, em um condomínio no bairro Portal do Sol; em um prédio empresarial no bairro Expedicionários; e em outro prédio empresarial no bairro dos Estados. Um computador e aparelhos celulares foram apreendidos.

Hytalo Santos e o marido são presos em São Paulo

Segundo o delegado responsável pela prisão, o casal estava em uma possível rota de fuga do Brasil. Após serem detidos, os dois ficaram inicialmente em uma cadeia pública de Carapicuíba e, por segurança, foram encaminhados para o Centro de Detenção Provisória 1 de Pinheiros, na Zona Oeste de São Paulo.

No dia seguinte, 16 de agosto, o Tribunal de Justiça da Paraíba negou o pedido de liberdade apresentado pela defesa de Hytalo e Israel. A defesa havia entrado com um habeas corpus, mas a liminar para a soltura dos dois foi negada.

O influencer paraibano Hytalo Santos e o marido dele, Israel Nata Vicente, presos preventivamente nesta sexta-feira (15) em uma casa em Carapicuíba, na Grande São Paulo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O pedido foi feito pelo Ministério Público do Trabalho para garantir o pagamento de uma eventual indenização por dano moral coletivo e medidas de reparação e assistência às vítimas, dentro da investigação trabalhista envolvendo o casal.

Segundo o MPT, havia indícios de ocultação de patrimônio, com movimentações financeiras consideradas atípicas e possíveis manobras de blindagem, ocultação e dissipação de bens. A Justiça aceitou os pedidos apresentados pelo órgão.

Hytalo Santos e Israel são transferidos para a Paraíba

Em 28 de agosto de 2025, Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente foram transferidos de São Paulo para a Paraíba. Os dois chegaram a João Pessoa e passaram por exames de corpo de delito no Instituto de Polícia Científica (IPC).

Uma equipe da Paraíba foi até São Paulo para buscar o casal. As passagens foram compradas ainda no dia 26 de agosto, segundo as autoridades.

Hytalo Santos chega em aeroporto na Paraíba, após transferência de SP — Foto: TV Cabo Branco

Em fevereiro de 2026, Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente foram condenados pela Justiça da Paraíba por produção de conteúdo pornográfico envolvendo adolescentes, crime previsto no Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente.

Hytalo foi condenado a 11 anos e 4 meses de prisão, enquanto Israel recebeu pena de 8 anos, 10 meses e 20 dias. As duas penas foram estabelecidas em regime inicialmente fechado e eles permanecem presos no presídio do Róger.

A sentença foi proferida pelo juiz Antônio Rudimacy Firmino de Sousa, da comarca de Bayeux, na Grande João Pessoa. A condenação ocorreu em primeira instância.

Hytalo Santos e marido são condenados — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Defesa pede anulação da condenação de Hytalo Santos

Hytalo Santos e seu marido durante depoimento à Justiça da Paraíba. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

Após a condenação, a defesa de Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente entrou com uma petição na Justiça da Paraíba para pedir a anulação da sentença que condenou os dois por produção de conteúdo pornográfico envolvendo adolescentes.

A defesa argumenta que a condenação considerou uma interpretação ampla do crime e cita a chamada “ECA Digital”, além do decreto que regulamenta a lei. Os advogados também afirmam que os conteúdos publicados pelos influenciadores são uma manifestação cultural ligada a movimentos periféricos, como o BregaFunk, e citam a proteção à liberdade de expressão cultural.

O pedido foi apresentado na Vara da Infância e Registro Público da Comarca Integrada de Bayeux e Santa Rita, na Grande João Pessoa.

Ainda não há prazo para apreciação da petição por parte do juiz do caso Hytalo Santos.

Casal é alvo de operação por lavagem de dinheiro

Em 1º de julho de 2026, Hytalo Santos e Israel Vicente foram alvos de uma operação que investiga lavagem de dinheiro e ocultação de patrimônio . Foram cumpridos cinco mandados de busca e apreensão em João Pessoa, Campina Grande e Recife.

Segundo o Gaeco, os valores investigados teriam origem em jogos e apostas ilegais, incluindo pagamentos em espécie ligados ao jogo do bicho. A apuração é um desdobramento da investigação sobre a exploração da imagem de crianças e adolescentes.

À época, a defesa afirmou ao g1 que Hytalo e Israel “jamais se recusaram a colaborar com a Justiça e sempre estiveram à disposição das autoridades para demonstrar sua clara inocência” .

Influenciador responde por outros 14 processos na Justiça da Paraíba

Além da condenação por produção de conteúdo pornográfico envolvendo adolescentes, H ytalo Santos é alvo de outros 14 processos na Justiça da Paraíba, nas áreas criminal e cível. Entre eles, há uma ação criminal por resistência e processos cíveis relacionados a direito de imagem, despesas condominiais, inadimplemento e outros assuntos.

Na Justiça do Trabalho, Hytalo e o marido, Israel Vicente, também são réus em uma ação por tráfico de pessoas para exploração sexual e trabalho em condições análogas à escravidão . Segundo o MPT-PB, há indícios de que menores eram levados para morar na residência do casal e submetidos a condições de trabalho, além de isolamento do convívio familiar e restrição de comunicação com o mundo externo.

Os detalhes dos 14 processos não estão disponíveis no sistema do Tribunal de Justiça da Paraíba. Também há registro de outros 14 processos já arquivados definitivamente pela Justiça estadual.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Election deadlock meets West Bank sieges, Gaza killings
articles.summary: As Israel grapples with an inconclusive election, Palestinians face West Bank closures and Gaza killings.
articles.body:
The election night highs for Palestinian citizens of Israel – Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats – turned into a week of delegitimising rhetoric from Israeli politicians.

Nearly 840,000 people voted for Ra’am and the Joint List, a 64 percent increase on 2022 , and adding them to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc would give an anti-Netanyahu coalition 67 seats; without them, only a unity deal between the main Zionist blocs or another election is possible.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud alleged the election had been “stolen” by Palestinian parties with unproven claims of Qatari financing. Qatar denied such accusations , as police sources told The Times of Israel that there was no evidence of widespread fraud. By Sunday, election committee chairman Noam Sohlberg declared the election “conducted properly”.

However, the rhetoric delegitimising the Palestinian vote is now being reflected in the coalition negotiations under way. Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beytenu party, has ruled out Palestinian partners, and Eisenkot has presented four conditions for anyone joining his coalition that would be anathema to the Palestinian parties, including recognising Israel as “a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state”, and mandatory national service for all citizens, including Palestinians.

However, Palestinian politicians continue to express a willingness to back an Eisenkot government from outside – if only to enable the departure of Netanyahu and the far right. Meanwhile, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv for a coalition that includes the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.

While the Israeli electorate was consumed by the election’s unclear results, Palestinians in the occupied West Bank continued enduring a variety of sieges, most prominently in Hebron. By October 29, Al Jazeera’s data unit counted 10 entrances sealed and about 5,000 people displaced. The city saw at least 120 arrests and 13 businesses demolished by Friday, when the army also blew up the homes of two men it blamed for an attack. Palestinian officials accused the government of using the operation to win settler votes ; no Israeli official has said so outright.

On November 2, Governor Khaled Dudin announced the army had withdrawn from Hebron, and that displaced families could return. The Jerusalem Post reported that the army’s chief of staff recommended leaving Hebron before the election, but that Netanyahu refused.

But even with the operation over, the damage remains following more than 120 arrests and daily economic losses the governor put at 10 million to 12 million shekels ($3.2m to $3.8m) in a city responsible for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output.

But Hebron was only the largest of many closures that continue to plague the West Bank. In Masafer Yatta, at least 12 villages were cut off , and the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that forces detained 10 teachers from the Jinba school on Sunday.

Yousef Shanaran – who has been besieged in his home with his family in Wadi Rakhim for four weeks now – told Al Jazeera on Monday that settlers have now poisoned the well outside his family home, which the family already was unable to access for days at a time due to the siege. “No water, no food, nothing at all I’ve got,” he said. “Nobody is allowed to bring anything to us.”

These sieges continue as settlers, and increasingly Israeli forces, disrupt the olive harvest across the West Bank. United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented 397 settler attacks causing casualties or damage in the first 26 days of October – a monthly high since OCHA began tracking such incidents in 2006.

Across villages, a familiar pattern has emerged: settlers attack pickers, the army declares a closed military zone and orders the farmers out, and the harvest is lost.

Amid reports of detentions and deportations of solidarity activists who came to the West Bank to assist in the olive harvest in recent days, activists accused settlers of assaulting three activist journalists at Umm al-Khair , and Israel revoked Brad Lander’s travel authorisation after he was detained while harvesting olives two weeks ago.

In Gaza, attacks continued on a daily basis as the UN human rights office warned on October 30 that Palestinians are being pushed into an ever smaller area, calling the “ Yellow Line ” a “kill zone” that is moving westward.

By November 2, the Ministry of Health put the death toll since last year’s ceasefire at 1,593. Sunday was the deadliest day of the week, with at least eight killed . Among those reported killed over the past week:

Government and police personnel were among those killed. On October 28, a drone strike on a Ministry of Economy facility in al-Mawasi, Rafah, where staff and security personnel had gathered, killed five people, including Ministry of Agriculture official Wajdi Abu Bakr, who died on Sunday from injuries sustained in the attack.

On November 1, a drone strike in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, killed five men whom Gaza’s Interior Ministry said were police officers.

Israeli attacks also killed children. Six-year-old Tahani Shalalfeh died of a gunshot wound in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, on October 27, and Yamen Saqr, eight, died on October 30 of wounds from Israeli fire in Khan Younis, according to Wafa and local activists. The young child Zain Owais was reported killed on November 1 with his father, Mohammed Ali Owais, and a third man in a strike near Taj Mall in Gaza City.

On October 27, a young man was killed in an air strike in west Rafah, and a member of the Bseiso family died of earlier wounds in Gaza City, Gaza Now reported. Mohammad al-Bayouk was killed in Khan Younis on October 28, and Mohammed al-Najjar was killed near Jabalia on Thursday.

On Friday, the body of a 47-year-old man killed in an air strike at al-Waha, north of Gaza City, was recovered, Wafa reported.

Ibrahim Saeed died on Sunday of wounds from tank fire in al-Musaddar, and Yusuf Abu Younis died Monday of wounds from a drone strike in Khan Younis the day before, according to local activist Hamza al-Masri.

On Monday, Mahmoud Qaffa and Asaad Qeshta were killed in separate air strikes in Khan Younis and Ibrahim al-Saayida, 40, in al-Musaddar, according to Wafa and Haaretz.

Israeli authorities claimed many of those killed this week were Hamas fighters, though no evidence was provided. Among those were Diaa Abu al-Rous, killed north of Nuseirat on Saturday, and Mohammed Qudeih, killed in a strike on a tent in Khan Younis the same day, who the military claimed were members of Hamas’s Nukhba Forces; Palestinian reports describe Abu al-Rous as a teacher.

Such killings take place with winter closing in and humanitarian conditions struggling to improve: two infant girls died of burns in a tent fire in al-Mawasi on Friday, and the shelter picture is dire , with Gaza’s Social Development Ministry saying about 200,000 tents are needed, yet only dozens have arrived due to Israeli entry restrictions.

With no hospitals in Gaza fully functioning, the Red Crescent warned on Monday that the health system is at risk of collapse after 26 hospitals went out of service – with fuel shortages threatening the remaining facilities.

articles.title: One dead after two helicopters collide near Mount Everest in Nepal
articles.summary: Authorities have confirmed that a 47-year-old Indian national was killed and two people injured.
articles.body:
Two helicopters have collided in Nepal’s Mount Everest region, killing at least one person and injuring two others.

The crash happened on Tuesday as both aircraft were attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp. Mount Everest is the world’s tallest mountain above sea level.

Footage posted online shows more than a dozen people running to safety as the helicopters crashed into the ground following a collision.

Authorities have confirmed that a 47-year-old Indian national was killed. A New Zealand national and a Nepali pilot were injured. It is not clear how many people were on board the two helicopters.

The crash happened in Pheriche village, at an altitude of 4,200 metres (13,780 feet).

The Mount Everest region can be difficult to navigate because there are no roads. Helicopters are regularly used to evacuate trekkers and guides who have had to cut their journeys short because of sickness or exhaustion. Temperatures on the mountain always remain below freezing.

Last week, a fire broke out at a hotel along the route to Mount Everest base camp. Heavy snowfall hampered efforts to extinguish the blaze.

No deaths or injuries were reported in the fire.

articles.title: Sam Fender enlists his old North Shields school for John Lewis ad
articles.summary: Sam Fender's chance meet with an old teacher gives North Shield's pupils the ultimate Christmas gig.
articles.body:
A chance encounter with an old music teacher ended with the "real shock" of Sam Fender's old school providing vocals for the John Lewis Christmas ad this year.

Without telling them Fender enlisted the help of current pupils at John Spence Community High School in North Shields to re-record the choir for his cover of the Rolling Stones classic You Can't Always Get What You Want.

Head of music at John Spence, Damien Grazzer, said the invitation was a "real shock" but it was an "amazing experience" for the children involved.

The singer also reunited with the Easington Colliery Band for the track after they worked together on his last album.

Fender said: "In the spirit of Christmas, we re-recorded the children's choir with the kids from my old school... and we arranged a brass section with the Easington Colliery Band."

Proceeds from the sale of the single, which includes Fender's 2020 cover of Winter Song, will go to the Teenage Cancer Trust and Action for Children.

Grazzer, who has worked at the school for more than 20 years, said the latest scholars became involved after he bumped into old boy Fender in the summer holidays.

"It came as a real shock to be honest," he said.

The pupils were not told what the recording was for and only had a day to rehearse, but Fender made an emotional appearance towards the end of the recording session.

"He even said just looking at the tie and the uniform really brought back his fondness for high school and his teachers," Grazzer said.

"What an amazing experience for those students, it's something that they'll never forget, it'll be there forever."

"Just to give something back like that I think is absolutely incredible."

Easington Colliery Band, who feature on the track Remember My Name on 2025's People Watching album, performed with Fender during his stadium tour last year.

Principal cornet player Dan Robson said the hardest thing was not being able to tell anyone about the latest collaboration.

"It's turned into a relationship more than just that kind of one job," Robson said.

"So when we got this phone call it was kind of like 'oh brilliant here we go again'."

He described the experience as "unbelievable", saying Fender "puts everything into everything".

articles.title: Beyond disaster relief: India-US Tiger Triumph exercise brings cyber, space into focus
articles.summary: India and the United States have begun the fifth edition of the bilateral Exercise Tiger Triumph in Visakhapatnam.
articles.body: India and the United States have begun the fifth edition of the bilateral Exercise Tiger Triumph in Visakhapatnam. The aim if this edition of the exercise is to improve interoperability for Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Response (HADR), tabletop staff planning and integrated multi-domain command and control. Tiger Triumph is the only tri-service exercise India takes part in apart from Exercise INDRA which is held with Russia.US Pacific Fleet vice commander Rear Admiral Joaquin Martinez de Pinillos said that the exercise reflects the "growing strength, sophistication and shared commitment" of the US-India major defense partnership. The American Admiral went on to add that the exercise sharpens combined operational coordination and prepares both forces to respond quickly to crises and natural disasters in the region. Rear Admiral Vishal Bishnoi, Flag Officer Commanding Eastern Fleet, said the exercise gives practical expression to the relationship by bringing together "complementary capabilities of our armed forces" in a demanding HADR settings.This edition of the exercise brings together staff planning, all-domain tabletop exercises and specialised command, control, cyber and space synchronisation. Personnel from both sides will also and hold subject-matter expert exchanges.From disaster relief to multi-domain planningThe exercise has grown steadily since its first edition in 2019 that was held at Visakhapatnam and Kakinada, was the first tri-service exercise India held with the US. The fourth edition took place in Visakhapatnam in April 2025. This year's emphasis on space, cyber and command and control shows how far the series is evolving.The exercise comes as both countries deepen their strategic partnership. They are part of the Quad with Japan and Australia, and of I2U2 with the UAE and Israel. New Delhi and Washington promote a free, open and secure Indo-Pacific, even as China grows more assertive in the region. Both India and China fall under the area of operations of the US Indo-Pacific Command, the largest US command by area.A widening defence relationshipIndia buys from Russia, the US, France, Israel and others while expanding domestic manufacturing. It operates American-origin platforms such as the C-17 and C-130J transports, P-8I maritime patrol aircraft, Apache and Chinook helicopters, MH-60R naval helicopters and M777 howitzers, and talks with Washington have extended to co-production and technology transfer. The sanctions after India's 1998 nuclear tests, and the possibility of action under CAATSA after the S-400 purchase, remain part of that background.High-level military contacts have been frequent. In the last year, the then chiefs of all three services visited the US. Admiral Dinesh K Tripathi, now retired, visited from November 12 to 17, 2025. Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, who retired recently, went from April 6, 2026, and General Upendra Dwivedi travelled in April 2026, a few months before his retirement.India conducts a large number of exercises with the US across services, among them Yudh Abhyas, Vajra Prahar, Malabar and Cope India, besides multilateral drills such as RIMPAC and Sea Dragon. Its role as an associate partner in the Combined Maritime Forces reflects shared maritime security priorities. Tiger Triumph 2026 adds another layer to that record, and the shift from disaster response to cyber and space planning suggests where the partnership is heading.

articles.title: How to follow the election on the BBC
articles.summary: Whether you plan to follow the US midterms on TV, radio or online, the BBC has you covered.
articles.body:
Voters in the US are casting their ballots in midterm elections, with the results set to shape the next two years of American politics.

BBC News is on hand to keep you up-to-date with the latest developments across all platforms, no matter where you are in the world.

Follow the election results and developments as the night unfolds on the BBC News website and app.

We'll stream the BBC's election results programme from 18:30 EST (23:30 GMT) once polls close on the East Coast.

It will also be available to watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC News YouTube .

There'll also be a comprehensive text and video offer and a live page where you can get the latest updates, reaction and analysis.

Audiences will be able to use the interactive results service to watch live updates of the vote count in every state.

Follow live updates on US midterm elections

The BBC's election results programme will be broadcast live from Washington on BBC One and the BBC News Channel from 18:30 EST (23:30 GMT).

It will be hosted by Clive Myrie from the Capitol, with Sumi Somaskanda and Caitríona Perry in the BBC's Washington DC studio.

Correspondents will report from battleground states while North America editor Sarah Smith and North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher will give their take from Washington DC.

BBC analysis editor Ros Atkins will also drill down into the key results as they come in.

BBC Breakfast will also have a round-up of the results for viewers on BBC One from 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday 4 November, with analysis of what it means for Donald Trump's final two years in office.

Special coverage from Washington starts at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT) with James Coomarasamy and Asma Khalid.

Listeners in the UK can follow them on BBC Radio 4 . Listeners outside the UK can hear the same broadcast on the BBC World Service .

The Today programme on BBC Radio 4 will have all the reaction to the night's events from Washington from 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday 4 November.

Election week also sees Americast become a daily podcast, with Justin Webb, Sarah Smith, Anthony Zurcher and Marianna Spring helping audiences make sense of the biggest moments.

The BBC has two trusted partners that provide results - AP news agency and our US news partner CBS.

When we bring you a result, we call it a "projection". That's because our partners analyse incoming results data, and when they are confident that one candidate has an unbeatable lead in a particular race, they project the winner.

That projection is not the official result - but it nearly always proves to be correct when all the votes are eventually counted.

The final result comes when states certify the results – often days or weeks after election day.

articles.summary: Shark Tank judge and Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal has questioned the country’s tax rules for Employee Stock Option Plans (ESOPs), saying employees are
articles.body: Shark Tank judge and Shaadi.com founder Anupam Mittal has questioned the country’s tax rules for Employee Stock Option Plans (ESOPs), saying employees are taxed heavily when they exercise their stock options and become shareholders. In a post on LinkedIn, Anupam Mittal argued that the tax system should encourage employee ownership instead of making it costly, especially as startups look to attract talent and create wealth. For those unaware, ESOPs allow employees to buy shares in a company at a fixed price, often giving them a chance to benefit as the business grows. However, when employees exercise their options, the difference between the purchase price and the market value of the shares is generally taxed as a salary perquisite at their applicable income tax rate.Anupam Mittal’s comments also come amid a recent Bengaluru Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) ruling involving a Flipkart employee. The tribunal held that proceeds from the company’s repurchase of vested but unexercised ESOPs could be taxed as long-term capital gains (LTCG), rather than as salary perquisites. However, the tax treatment depends on the structure and circumstances of the transaction.Here’s what Anupam Mittal saidSharing his views on X, Mittal wrote:“Why does India punish employee ownership?We keep telling employees - Think like an owner.Then we tax them for becoming one 🤷🏻Say you get ESOPs at ₹10.You exercise when the share is worth ₹100. That ₹90 appreciation can be taxed as a perquisite at your marginal rate, potentially ~40%.Why should emp wealth be treated less favourably than long-term wealth created by public or private investors?ESOPs aren’t compensation alone.They are how startups turn employees into owners, align incentives and spread wealth creation beyond founders and investors.If we believe India needs more startups, more employment generation & more wealth creation....then perhaps we should encourage ESOP ownership, not something we need tax lawyers for.Cheat code - If you can get your co to buy back your ESOPS instead of exercising them, recent case law suggests the gain qualifies for LTCG”You use AI every day. articles.title: DUP leader Gavin Robinson 'very sorry' Carla Lockhart has quit the party
articles.summary: Gavin Robinson said the party and the Upper Bann MP agreed on the sentiment but not the strategy of sanctioning Sinn Féin.
articles.body:
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson has said he is "very sorry" that MP Carla Lockhart has quit the party.

Robinson said he would not be criticising the Upper Bann MP, who left the party on Monday over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute , and expressed hope they would continue to work together in the future.

Lockhart had been calling for the DUP to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the Garvaghy Road demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.

But Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.

Speaking on the Good Morning Ulster programme he said: "We share exactly the same sentiment - all of us are angered, all of us believe the position of Michelle O'Neill and her willingness to break the law, to ignore the courts, to breach her pledge of office requires sanction.

"So while we share the same sentiment, we have not been in agreement when it comes to how you deal with it.

"The Democratic Unionist Party is firmly of the view that it is Michelle O'Neill who should face the consequences of her actions, not the rest of the people of Northern Ireland.

"Northern Ireland needs a functioning government, Northern Ireland needs a budget - those important discussions will continue on Thursday I believe with the secretary of state."

Robinson said he believes "there is a role for this government to come forward with a sanctions regime that will punish those who break the pledge of office".

Speaking after a meeting of the Northern Ireland Executive, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly reiterated DUP calls for "unionist cooperation" and warned that unionism was "weakened by infighting".

Little-Pengelly said the unionist community felt "anger and frustration" over Sinn Féin's response to Drumcree and the Irish republican party had "fractured" relations within Northern Ireland's power-sharing government.

O'Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president, has defended her involvement in the Drumcree protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".

In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said forcing O'Neill from office was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".

In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.

"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."

Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.

"I cannot stand idly by whilst Sinn Féin wilfully ignores the rule of law and the promised profound consequences fail to materialise," she added.

Lockhart concluded that she would "look forward to working with all shades of unionism, elected or not, to advance the cause we love".

A local councillor has also quit the party.

Clement Cuthbertson, a councillor for Dungannon in Mid Ulster District Council, has been a DUP member for 30 years and will continue his elected role on the council as an independent unionist.

"I have reached the point where remaining a party member would mean asking people to accept a position I cannot defend," he said in a social media post.

A DUP spokesperson said: "We regret Clement Cuthbertson's decision to resign from the party and wish him well for the future."

The DUP MP for East Londonderry Gregory Campbell said Lockhart's resignation had come as no surprise and could prove a "pivotal moment" for the wider unionist family.

"Do we advance the cause of unionism by fracturing or closing ranks and uniting and trying to get people together to say 'what is the best way forward, what's the best way to set out a strategy what will maximise the pro-union voice?'," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"Fracturing only assists those who are the enemies of unionism, uniting will thwart the enemies of unionism and that's what we need to do and I think that realisation is going to come home now in the next few weeks."

MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row

Speaking on the Good Morning Ulster programme on Tuesday, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister said the DUP had "preferred to keep Michelle O'Neill and let Carla Lockhart go" and that would "hang over them and haunt them for some time to come".

He added: "I have both publicly and privately made it very plain that Carla would be very welcome in the TUV, but I understand Carla's position.

"When you've been in a party as she has and indeed as I was for 20 years and then you leave it, it's quite a step."

Also on Tuesday, Sinn Féin Finance Minister John O'Dowd said the DUP needs to "set party politics aside" as the executive works to agree a budget.

He was speaking after ministers met ahead of further talks with the secretary of state later this week.

O'Dowd said all ministers need to remain focused on the task at hand, and that he will present further options to them about what is possible in the coming days.

There is the prospect of strike action by health workers if they do not get a long-awaited pay deal that cannot be released without a budget.

O'Dowd said the primary task was to ensure strikes are avoided, adding: "We are reaching a crunch period in relation to the discussions around the executive table and the terms and conditions with the British government."

On the absence of a Stormont budget and further talks this week with the secretary of state, Little-Pengelly said that "we are in a better position than where we were" but there was "still a significant gap".

articles.title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
articles.summary: The home secretary says the full cost of dropping plans to extend the wait for settlement will be laid out in future.
articles.body:
The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.

But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.

While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.

In March, the Home Office said the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.

Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.

She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".

Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.

Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.

Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.

In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.

"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.

"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.

The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.

While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.

The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.

The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which found a £115bn addition to UK public finances under current settlement rules.

"Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.

Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".

She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.

The exact wait will vary based on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.

Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had said it amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts" , while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.

articles.title: Coventry City fan, 14, arrested following Bradley Lowery taunt
articles.summary: Police are investigating an incident at Coventry's Premier League match with Sunderland on Saturday.
articles.body:
A 14-year-old boy has been arrested on suspicion of a public order offence and subsequently bailed, after a video on social media appeared to show a Coventry City fan taunting opposition Sunderland fans with a photo of Bradley Lowery.

Sunderland fan Bradley, who died aged six in 2017 after being diagnosed with a rare childhood cancer, captured the hearts of the football world.

The 14-year-old handed himself into West Midlands Police, who said they were investigating the incident.

The Sky Blues added they were also investigating the footage from Saturday's Premier League match and Bradley's mother, Gemma, issued an emotional statement.

"So much of Bradley's short life was spent battling cancer and enduring treatments no child should ever face," she posted on Instagram.

"To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt."

Her "beautiful boy deserves to be remembered with love, not hate," Lowery said in an update through the Bradley Lowery Foundation, which raises funds and awareness to help and support children with cancer.

She added she did not want hatred directing at the teenager involved, but instead wanted him to learn from his actions.

A spokesperson for the club said: "Coventry City FC is aware of footage circulating on social media in connection with an incident during our Premier League fixture against Sunderland [on Saturday]."

"The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action."

West Midlands Police added they understood the upset the video had caused and were keeping Bradley's family updated as the investigation continued.

articles.title: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall on India’s eastern coast
articles.summary: Severe cyclonic storm uproots trees and downs power lines, days after another cyclone battered the same region.
articles.body:
Cyclone Murasu has made landfall on India’s eastern coast, uprooting trees, toppling electricity poles and flooding low-lying areas in Andhra Pradesh. It is the second cyclone to strike the region in a week after Cyclone Arnab .

The severe cyclonic storm came ashore near Ongole in Prakasam district about 1am on Tuesday (19:30 GMT on Monday), according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

The IMD warned of heavy to very heavy rain across several districts through the day.

No deaths or injuries have been reported so far, Prakhar Jain, the managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told the Reuters news agency. He said some trees and electricity poles had been uprooted.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency reported extensive damage in Prakasam and Bapatla districts, where thousands of trees were felled, hundreds of power poles damaged and fishing boats wrecked. Standing crops were also hit, and many areas were underwater.

Authorities began evacuating people on Monday and planned to move about 30,000 people to safety in Andhra Pradesh, Jain said.

“This is the most dangerous cyclone we have witnessed in the last 14 years,” Krishnamma, a fisherman from Kothapatnam in Prakasam district, told PTI. He said about 400 families from his village had been moved out before the storm hit.

Indian Home Minister Amit Shah said on X that he had spoken to Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu about the cyclone’s impact.

“I assured him that the Central Government will provide all kinds of assistance and support,” Shah wrote, adding that national and state disaster response teams were already on the ground.

Murasu formed over the Bay of Bengal, which regularly spawns deadly storms on India’s east coast. It comes days after Cyclone Arnab caused heavy damage in Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring Odisha.

The IMD forecast that Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu to its south would be worst hit. Murasu is also causing heavy rain in Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Odisha.

The prospect of higher costs and tighter restrictions has also fuelled fears that American companies could become less willing to hire overseas talent.The pressure extends beyond the H-1B programme. The administration has replaced the traditional random H-1B lottery with a weighted selection system that favours higher-paid and higher-skilled applicants, while proposing higher prevailing-wage requirements. It has also expanded social-media screening to H-1B applicants and their H-4 dependents, requiring them to make their online profiles publicly accessible for vetting.For thousands of Indian professionals and their families, these changes mean greater uncertainty over employment, visa renewals and chance at naturalised citizenship.These concerns make Trump's immigration approach particularly consequential for a community with a significant foreign-born population.The Carnegie survey found that 64% of Indian-Americans disapproved of his handling of immigration.While the study does not isolate H-1B visa policy as a separate voting issue, the broader dissatisfaction reflects the political sensitivity of immigration in a community whose professional and personal lives are closely intertwined with America's migration system.The economyEconomic performance is another major source of dissatisfaction with the Trump administration. For Indian-Americans, as for voters across the United States, the domestic economy is an important measure of presidential performance.The Carnegie survey found that 68% of Indian-Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of domestic economic policy. This assessment covered issues including inflation, taxes and government spending. Economic policy is not a niche concern affecting one section of the community. It is a broad measure of how voters assess the administration's ability to manage their everyday financial circumstances.The economy also complicates the Republican Party's efforts to retain the support it gained among Indian-Americans in 2024. Trump's appeal to some sections of the community was part of a wider shift that narrowed the Democrats' traditional advantage. But dissatisfaction with his administration's economic management has weakened the prospects of converting those gains into lasting political support.Trade and tariffsInternational economic policy is another area where Trump faces considerable opposition among Indian-Americans.The Carnegie survey found that 70% disapproved of his handling of international economic policy, including trade, tariffs and sanctions. This was the highest disapproval figure among the three broad policy areas examined in the survey.For a community with strong professional, commercial and family connections across national borders, international economic decisions can carry consequences beyond diplomatic disagreements.Trade policy, tariffs and sanctions form part of the wider economic relationship between the United States and the rest of the world. They also influence the environment in which businesses, professionals and international partnerships operate.The finding is particularly important because it suggests that dissatisfaction with Trump is not restricted to domestic economic management or immigration. His administration's approach to the global economy is also facing resistance within a community that has traditionally maintained strong international connections.Republican gains among Indian-Americans in 2024 demonstrated that the community was not immune to Trump's economic and political messaging. But the latest findings indicate that those gains have proved difficult to sustain.US-India relationsThe state of US-India relations is another issue shaping the political mood among Indian-Americans, although it is important not to overstate its electoral significance.For years, the strengthening of ties between Washington and New Delhi was viewed positively by many in the Indian-American community. The relationship had become an important part of the broader narrative of India's growing international influence and the diaspora's increasing political visibility in the United States.But Trump's second term has brought fresh uncertainty to the relationship.The Carnegie survey found that large majorities of Indian-Americans disapproved of Trump's handling of US-India relations, which had once been a relative strength for him. This is particularly notable because the community's assessment of the president's performance on India has deteriorated alongside its views on immigration and economic policy.However, there is an important caveat. The October 2026 survey does not provide a separate percentage ranking US-India relations among voters' most important election issues. It establishes dissatisfaction with the administration's handling of the relationship, not that foreign policy is necessarily a decisive factor in the congressional vote.The survey, however, notes that Indian-Americans may be concerned about the direction of bilateral ties, but their electoral decisions are not necessarily driven by what happens between Washington and New Delhi.Identity and belongingBeyond conventional policy questions, Indian-Americans are increasingly finding themselves at the centre of a debate about national identity and belonging.The Carnegie report points to an incident that brought these tensions into sharp focus ahead of the midterms. Republican candidate Bo French, running for state office in Texas, posted a photograph of University of Texas students of visibly South Asian origin celebrating their football team's success.His accompanying remark — questioning whether the university's graduation ceremony looked like the photograph — ignited a debate about the place of Indian-Americans in American society.The controversy showed how questions of immigration, identity and belonging can become intertwined.Indian-Americans number fewer than six million and constitute approximately 1.5% of the US population. Nevertheless, the debate provides an important backdrop to the midterm elections. For Indian-Americans, the political conversation is not confined to taxation, economic performance or immigration rules. It also concerns how comfortably they feel represented and accepted in the country they call home.The Republican problemPerhaps the most consequential finding of the Carnegie survey is not about any single policy issue but the extent to which Indian-American voters appear to be moving away from Republican candidates. articles.title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges
articles.summary: Supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden  and Belgium reported fridges being hiked in temperature on Monday.
articles.body:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October .

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.

The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.

Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".

"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"

"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."

So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.

But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.

"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.

Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.

Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.

"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.

"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

articles.title: 143-year-old Pittsburgh paint company finds its biggest boom as Microsoft, Google, Amazon build AI data centres; gray paint sales to data centres set to triple; VP says: “I’ve never seen a…
articles.summary: PPG, a 143-year-old Pittsburgh company that started out making glass, has found an unlikely growth engine in AI data centres.
articles.body: PPG, a 143-year-old Pittsburgh company that started out making glass, has found an unlikely growth engine in AI data centres. The firm expects its paint sales to data centres to triple this year from last year, The New York Times reported. The coatings are mostly gray and they do a serious job, shielding steel from fire, rust and static electricity inside the huge facilities that Microsoft, Google, Amazon and other tech giants are racing to build. "I've never seen a boom as big as this," said Jenn Solcz, PPG's vice president of protective and marine coatings for the Americas.The surge stands out against the rest of the business. PPG's total sales rose 7% to $4.5 billion in the most recent quarter, and data centres still make up only a low-single-digit share of sales in two parts of the company, executives told the Times. Amy Ericson, a PPG senior vice president, expects data centres to grow "multiple times" faster than other infrastructure markets.Data centre paint sales are outrunning PPG's overall growthRival Sherwin-Williams is seeing a similar pull. Its chief executive, Heidi Petz, said in July that its protective and marine sales rose by a midteens percentage from a year earlier, helped by data centre construction.Speed is a big part of the pitch. Data centres go up in about a third of the time a typical infrastructure project takes, Solcz said, so PPG built one team for the tech giants and another that works with architects and builders before construction begins. The aim is to get its coatings written into a project's approved materials list early.In April, PPG rolled out a data centre package at a trade show in Washington. It covers steel fireproofing, rust-resistant primers, anti-static flooring and coatings that block electrical interference between machines. The company also makes coatings for more than 75 data centre parts, including security camera housings and cooling equipment.Steelguard 951 swells into a crust that keeps fire away from steelThe flagship product is Steelguard 951. At PPG's test facility near Pittsburgh, researchers aimed torches at coated steel panels inside a concrete building called "the bunker." Paul Fenton, a PPG chemist, held up one panel where a 1 mm layer of paint had swollen into a black crust almost 10 mm tall. Trapped air keeps the steel cool, he said, "just like a toasted marshmallow."The coating can protect steel for up to four hours, which gives people time to get out. Fires at data centres can start at backup generators, batteries or nearby power plants.Looks barely matter. PPG's shades are named light gray, gray and dark gray, and data centres are filled with machines, not people. Pipes are the exception, with blue for chilled water and red for sprinklers. Matthew Giddings of real estate firm JLL said paint can cost $3 million to $8 million for one building, a sliver of construction costs.There are bumps ahead. Some projects are waiting on power, transformer shortages have stretched timelines, and local opposition is growing. Ericson said the backlash is for tech companies and utilities to handle.PPG began in 1883 as the Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company. In 2024, it sold its US and Canadian paint-store business, including the Glidden brand, and now mostly serves businesses, coating cars, aircraft and beverage cans.You use AI every day. articles.title: US hits Qeshm Island, Pezeshkian signals more diplomacy: Iran war latest
articles.summary: With the first US attack on Qeshm Island since June, Iran and the US are on parallel tracks towards both peace and war.
articles.body:
Amid growing concerns about renewed attacks on Iran following Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, US forces have struck Iran’s Qeshm Island in what officials have reportedly described as a defensive measure.

In the first attack since June on Qeshm Island, which serves as the primary platform for Iran’s “asymmetric” naval power , according to analysts, the US strikes come as both sides continue to adopt military and diplomatic postures.

Mediation efforts led by Qatar are continuing in a bid to avert a return to all-out war, which began on February 28 when the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran, triggering the closure of the critical Strait of Hormuz, surging oil and gas prices and massive damage to military, civil and energy facilities around the Gulf.

What happened in the attack on Qeshm Island?

Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island late on Monday, as US media reported that the US military had carried out what officials called “defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz.

The blasts came in rapid succession, according to Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency. Witnesses told the agency they saw two planes flying over the island, located off Iran’s southern coast along the waterway.

According to The Wall Street Journal, which quoted an unnamed official, the strikes on Monday night appeared limited and were not a resumption of a major operation.

The Associated Press news agency also quoted an unnamed US official as saying Washington had conducted the defensive strikes against “Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”.

The attack came after IRNA reported that the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US first struck a critical desalination plant on Qeshm Island on March 7 – one week into the war. The strike, which Tehran branded a “flagrant crime” against civilians, cut off freshwater supplies to 30 surrounding villages.

It is, but it is fragile, and mixed messages are coming from both sides.

Qatari mediators have been engaged in indirect talks with Iranian officials in recent days. They have passed messages between the two sides, but the talks appeared to come to an end on Monday with no news of a breakthrough.

An official briefed on the talks told the Reuters news agency that Iran’s delegation had departed from Doha on Sunday, but that a draft proposal was still being circulated, without elaborating on the content.

Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi regarding a version of a draft US-Iran deal which has been under negotiation for the past eight days, an official told Reuters.

Araghchi told IRNA on Monday: “Consultations through mediators are very intensive. We have presented our conditions and proposals, and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington.”

Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also told a news conference on Monday that the “ball” was in the US’s court as Iran’s demands were “clear and logical”.

He said the plan Iran submitted in September to end the war remained the focus of talks, but that the proposal could be shortened and implemented in “two days”, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to talks about Iran’s nuclear programme.

On Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had given the government “certain authorities” over talks with the US, local media reported.

The president added that Tehran would look to resolve the conflict through dialogue.

Khamenei’s apparent approval of diplomacy marks a change since the breakdown of the June memorandum of understanding , which allowed a brief ceasefire and peace negotiations, when the supreme leader said the US could not be trusted.

For the US side, Vice President JD Vance also told reporters on Monday that he was hopeful for a diplomatic solution – just hours before the strikes on Qeshm Island.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance said. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Iran’s response to any US “miscalculation”, such as launching strikes, would be unpredictable.

“The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military action, but they are sorely mistaken; Iran will not submit,” he said.

Oil prices dropped by more than 7 percent on Monday. In response, Trump wrote on his Truth Social account that people believe the war with Iran will not resume as mediation efforts continue.

“Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!” Trump wrote.

He told media at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, that it looked like efforts were “coming together very nicely”.

“That’s why I guess the oil prices dropped. People found out about it.”

However, Trump also told the US media outlet Axios before his post on Truth Social that he was “in no rush” to decide whether to resume strikes on Iran.

“One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline, and their people are getting very tired of it,” Trump told Axios in an interview.

The US midterm elections are being viewed as the inflexion point for Trump’s decision on what path he takes next.

The president has suggested several times that he could attack Iran following the vote and told the Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) on Sunday that the conflict would end “very soon one way or the other”, adding that Tehran would either “make a deal, or we’ll just end it”.

Observers say the US will likely renew strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities if they do resume.

In particular, this could include Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a highly fortified site that contains two tunnel complexes buried deep underground, and which Trump told US outlet Newsmax last month could be a target. He said the US “may have to go there. We’ll take a shot at that one. We’ll knock it out fast.”

articles.summary: A High Court judge has ruled in favour of a claimant in a dispute over assets belonging to a deceased man after finding that certain transactions amounted
articles.body: A High Court judge has ruled in favour of a claimant in a dispute over assets belonging to a deceased man after finding that certain transactions amounted to gifts made in contemplation of death. The case involved Masudur Rahman and four defendants, who disputed the ownership of assets belonging to the late Al-Hasib Mian Muhammad Abdullah Al Mahmood.On 30 May 2024, the court held that the transactions qualified as donationes mortis causa, a legal term for gifts made in anticipation of death. A further judgment on 1 August 2024 dealt with the assets covered by the decision, legal costs and the defendants’ applications for permission to appeal. According to The National Archives, the court also clarified which bank accounts were excluded from the ruling.Which UK assets were included in Rahman’s claim over gifts made before deathThe dispute concerned assets that the deceased was alleged to have given to Rahman on 15 and/or 20 October 2020. The claim covered property in the United Kingdom and bank accounts, excluding property in Bangladesh. The court’s May judgment found that certain transactions met the requirements for gifts made in contemplation of death.However, the later hearing addressed whether 11 additional bank accounts listed in a draft order were also covered. Rahman argued that they were included. The defendants disagreed. His Honour Judge Paul Matthews, sitting as a High Court judge, said those accounts had not been specifically listed in the relevant claim documents. He ruled that the earlier decision applied only to the assets pleaded in the claim, not every UK asset the deceased had discussed.Why did the judge grant permission to appeal on five groundsThe defendants sought permission to challenge the May ruling on eight grounds. These included arguments about whether land certificates, lease copies, online banking passwords and bank cards could indicate title to assets. They also questioned the judge’s approach to the deceased’s intention to make a gift. Judge Matthews found no real prospect of success on grounds one, six and seven.However, he said grounds two to five had a real prospect of success because they raised legal questions. He also accepted that ground eight raised novel issues about applying the doctrine to registered land and bank accounts accessed through online passwords and bank cards. Permission to appeal was granted on grounds two to five and eight. The decision did not overturn the earlier ruling.Why did the court order the defendants to pay Rahman’s legal costsThe judge ruled that Rahman was the successful party overall, although he had not obtained everything he claimed. The defendants accepted that assessment. Rahman had made a settlement offer in January 2023, proposing that he receive a house, its furniture and personal belongings, and all bank accounts. The court later awarded him two flats instead of the furniture and personal effects.Judge Matthews considered the flats worth far more and found the outcome at least as advantageous as the offer. The defendants were therefore liable for costs on the standard basis before 14 February 2023 and on the indemnity basis afterwards, with interest and an additional amount under the relevant court rules.Defendants ordered to pay £259,725 towards legal costsThe court dismissed Rahman’s application to increase his approved costs budget, which stood at £320,648.50 plus applicable VAT. It nevertheless ordered the defendants to pay £259,725.29, plus applicable VAT, as an interim payment towards costs within 14 days. Permission to appeal was conditional on that payment being made by the deadline.If the defendants pursued ground eight, they also had to pay 50% of Rahman’s appeal costs regardless of the outcome. The judge limited Rahman’s right to an account of the estate to the assets found to have been given to him. He dismissed his claim for interest on £650,000, but ordered that interest earned on the relevant accounts be accounted for.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court documents. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims, asset details, settlement terms, or financial assessments mentioned. The information reflects the court's findings and should not be interpreted as confirmation of any details beyond those recorded in the judgment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: DJ 'never enjoyed exercise at school' ahead of 400-mile bike feat
articles.summary: Radio host Owain Wyn Evans hopes Children in Need bike challenge will inspire others to 'make a change'.
articles.body:
Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans has admitted he "never enjoyed exercise at school" because of bullying, ahead of his four nations biking challenge for Children in Need.

The host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show is set to cycle almost 400 miles over five days , setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff.

Evans, 42, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, begins his challenge in Scotland on 9 November, concluding the 643km feat in the Welsh capital on 13 November.

"Mentally, for me, it's been a challenge," said Evans. "Hopefully I'm going to inspire people to do exercise and realise that you can do this; you don't have to write off exercise forever."

"This is going to be really difficult for me personally, 100%," acknowledged Evans, who is undertaking his second challenge for the BBC charity fundraiser, following his 24-hour drumathon challenge back in 2021 .

"I never had a good relationship with exercise when I was in school," the Welsh radio host said.

"I was bullied and I found going into a changing room, football field or rugby pitch... were places I didn't feel safe when I was growing up.

He said he hoped "people who are seeing me do this, understand that this is a tough one for me".

"And maybe there will be people watching this now who think, 'yeah when I was in school I didn't like PE...'," said Evans who remembered "never fitting in in some way".

"For me, as a 42-year-old man, who's had that experience for his whole life, I guess I am now realising that you can make a change in your life and you can make a difference.

"It's taken a while, but this challenge is what has helped me reach this point," he said.

"It's a four-nation, 400-mile cycle challenge... all of those things are alien to me," said Evans, who didn't even own a bike before the current challenge.

"I'm not a cyclist. I'm not an endurance athlete in any way, shape or form - and when I was asked to do this, of course I said yes, because I love Children in Need and have an existing relationship with them."

However, he added: " I did think - gulp - am I going to be able to do this? And that's been a bit of a recurring thing for me ever since.

"Am I good enough? Am I going to be able to do this? Will I succeed? Will I finish?"

He described Children in Need as "an incredible charity - we're so lucky to have it", but he stressed the extent of the support required, with the annual fundraiser only able "to help one out of the six projects that approach it".

Reflecting on his months of training, Evans said: "I think, for me, the hurdles are the hills. I think the distance stuff I'm kind of ok with, but you never know how long or how steep a hill is going to be.

"One of the worst things I did was look at the weather forecast for the challenge week, because it looks like it's going to be cold, wet and windy - famously not good conditions for cyclists.

"But it is what it is. Being a weather presenter for so many years - back in the day - I know there's one thing about the weather you can't do, and that's change it!"

The BBC said Evans' challenge would be the "greatest ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

After cycling through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales, Evans said bringing the challenge to a close in Cardiff will be "special".

"That was something I wanted to happen from the very beginning, so I think it will be a very emotional moment - arriving in Cardiff on that final morning."

Despite having worked all over the UK, he said: "I've always thought I'd like to return to Wales, because I believe we Welsh people tend to want to come back home.

"This feeling of hiraeth is very real, and I certainly felt it while I was away."
