articles.title: US intelligence gaps widen as CIA-ODNI feud slows sharing on Iran, global threats
articles.summary: The sharing of US intelligence on Iran and other global threats with Congress and government agencies has slowed, with some exchanges temporarily halted,
articles.body: The sharing of US intelligence on Iran and other global threats with Congress and government agencies has slowed, with some exchanges temporarily halted, during US president Donald Trump's second term, eight current and former officials briefed on the matter told news agency Reuters.Former officials and intelligence experts have warned that the disruptions could leave policymakers without a complete picture of threats facing the US. They say the situation brings back concerns about intelligence failures exposed after the September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda attacks.The slowdown comes as the Trump administration considers whether to resume military strikes on Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections.The problems began during Tulsi Gabbard's tenure as director of national intelligence, when her office was locked in a major dispute with the CIA. Although tensions have eased since Gabbard resigned in June, the fallout continues to affect intelligence-sharing arrangements, two US officials familiar with the matter said.The CIA has stopped jointly preparing assessments with the National Intelligence Council (NIC), an analytical body within the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI). This has reduced the number of reports that bring together the views of different intelligence agencies for senior officials and policymakers, including on issues such as Iran.Lawmakers and their staff also briefly stopped receiving intelligence reports from Gabbard's office following the US military intervention in Iran in June 2025 and again after the capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January 2026, two people familiar with the matter said. Gabbard's team had accused lawmakers of leaking information to the press.The disruption in intelligence sharing has not been previously reported.CIA-ODNI feud hits intelligence assessmentsThe problems within the intelligence community emerged last year as the Trump administration cut staff and resources at national security agencies, including the ODNI and the CIA, while removing or sidelining officials it considered disloyal.The dispute between the CIA and the ODNI, two of the country's most important intelligence agencies, became one of the biggest turf battles in three decades, according to officials. The ODNI was established after the September 11 attacks to improve coordination among intelligence agencies.The rift began after Gabbard's office revoked the security clearances of serving and former intelligence officials about a year ago. It became so serious that White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles had to step in several times to ease tensions, three former officials said.One major consequence was the CIA's decision to stop contributing to assessments prepared by the National Intelligence Council. For decades, the council has helped lawmakers and government officials understand international developments and make foreign policy decisions.The NIC's reports are designed to combine the views of all 18 US intelligence agencies. The council had relied heavily on the CIA for analysis of countries such as Iran and Russia.The CIA continued to share intelligence with the council and contributed to some reports, but its analysts began focusing on assessments produced independently by the agency.The NIC, already affected by staff cuts, has since slowed the production of its reports, two people familiar with the matter said. Five current and former officials said none of its assessments had focused on the war in Iran.A CIA spokesperson, Liz Lyons, said the agency "participates fully" in preparing intelligence assessments through the Presidential Daily Brief, which is led by the ODNI, and through the NIC.An ODNI official said the council had maintained assessment levels close to "historic trendlines"."While Tulsi did not utilize the NIC, DNI Clayton has proven to be a good steward of the IC and recognizes the value of the NIC," a US official said, referring to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.Analysts fear political pressureSome former intelligence officials say analysts are increasingly cautious about producing assessments that might contradict the White House's position, fearing political retaliation. Two former officials and a serving US official said this was happening, although they did not identify the subjects on which analysts were avoiding taking a different position."Analysts still do the work, but this White House has made them irrelevant because the president treats unwelcome information as disloyalty," said Julia Curlee, a former CIA analyst who said she was fired from Trump's National Security Council last year for being transgender.Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence during Trump's first term, said the weakening of intelligence coordination could make it harder for policymakers to understand complex global threats.“All of these things are adding up in a really complex world where policymakers need to have a more sophisticated, nuanced, and integrated view of the world, and they are getting less,” she said.Morgan Muir, who served as deputy director of national intelligence under former President Joe Biden and also briefed President George W. Bush, warned that the breakdown of coordination could leave officials relying on separate sources of information rather than a common assessment."The problem is that by taking actions which have the effect of hollowing out institutions where there's actual intelligence community coordination on things, you're creating little lily pads, and then everybody can pick their own lily pad to listen to,” he said.FBI clashes with counterterrorism centreThe intelligence-sharing problems have also affected congressional briefings. Gabbard's office stopped briefing lawmakers on threats to US elections in 2025, according to two people familiar with the matter and a former US official.Clayton, who took over as director of national intelligence in August, has since restarted those briefings, officials said."Director Clayton remains committed to ensuring that ODNI and the intelligence community have the resources they need to continue informing key US government decision-makers and keeping Americans safe," the ODNI said in a statement to Reuters.A separate dispute also disrupted cooperation between the FBI and the National Counterterrorism Center (NCTC).The FBI stopped sharing some intelligence with the centre for several weeks late last year after its then-head, Joe Kent, and his staff tried to investigate the shooting of Charlie Kirk, the founder of Turning Point USA, two former officials said.FBI leaders told Kent they believed the NCTC was exceeding its authority. The FBI did not respond to a request for comment.Meanwhile, four former US officials said they were working on a bipartisan basis at Stanford University's Hoover Institution to develop proposals for rebuilding the intelligence community under the next administration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Random Musing | US Midterms 2026: Why neither MAGA nor Democrats are particularly bothered about Indian-Americans
articles.summary: Exploring the lack of political engagement and representation for Indian-Americans in the 2026 US Midterms, this article highlights their challenges with both major parties and the disconnect between their voting preferences and genuine political support.
articles.body: That minority groups are often used by progressives as a political football is evident to all, but no one summed it up as sharply as Malcolm X, who observed: “The white liberal differs from the white conservative only in one way: the liberal is more deceitful than the conservative. The liberal is more hypocritical than the conservative. Both want power, but the white liberal is the one who has perfected the art of posing as the Negro's friend and benefactor.”Today, the average Indian-American voter finds herself in a similar conundrum, except that, unlike the African-American voters of yore, neither liberals nor conservatives – with a few honourable exceptions – even care to pay lip service to earn a few brownie points.Consider how little noise the American political machine – on both sides of the aisle – made when a potential massacre was averted because a crazy 19-year-old's rifle jammed in the parking lot of a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago.As the midterms arrives, Indian-Americans find themselves in familiar territory: between a rock and a hard place, staring into the abyss of political irrelevance. Despite being one of the richest immigrant groups in the country, Indian-Americans may feel that America has rarely been more hostile towards them.On one side are MAGA’s open racists, who see Indian-American students enjoying a football game and imagine a great replacement in a strange iteration of the Tebbit Test, where even loyalty to one’s new land cannot overcome skin pigmentation.On the flip side are the Democrats, who, despite claiming to stand for minority rights, can’t even call Indians by their proper name, referring to them as “South Asians”, and are wont to platform people who are usually found at Dismantle Global Hindutva conferences.It’s a delicious twist of Shakespeare’s tongue that, after labelling Native Americans as “Indians”, so much of the American commentariat likes to call Indians “South Asians”. Unfortunately for us, when white folks make a faux pas, it lives on through history as the correct term.As Pushpita Prasad, an Indian-American community leader, pointed out to TOI Digital: “It’s frankly disrespectful to try and roll an India label into something else. India is a massive and historical label. Yet in 2020, Kamala Harris, the daughter of an Indian woman, gets called South Asian, while Jill Biden's Italian American heritage is respectfully used, even though her family immigrated in 1900.”Prasad also made a similar point about Diwali in a 2022 essay for the Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA), co-authored with Smitha Raj, arguing that rebranding the Dharmic religious festival as a generic “South Asian” celebration amounted to cultural appropriation and erased its religious roots.New Jews to New ZionistsThe sobriquet "South Asian" vacillates wildly depending on the context.A dish invented in India becomes Pakistani or South Asian; grooming gangs, on the other hand, earn the South Asian label.Anti-India hatred in Texas is labelled rising hatred of South Asians, while caste is always an Indian problem, as is “Hindu nationalism”, which is always rising and is almost always blamed for every evil in the world when it cannot be explained by Zionism or white supremacy. Twenty-six years after Jagdish Bhagwati named Indian-Americans the “new Jews”, Hindus are now often labelled the “new Zionists”.In fact, the caste bogey has been so prevalent in American discourse that California Democrats tried to push through a specific caste-discrimination bill that was eventually buried by Governor Gavin Newsom – ostensibly after a quiet word from the White House – because common sense prevailed and grown-ups realised that California didn’t have a raging caste issue.The more under-reported irony of that particular kerfuffle was that the campaign was spearheaded by Equality Labs, whose caste-sensitivity material was examined in a 2024 NCRI-Rutgers study. The researchers found that exposure to the material actually increased prejudice rather than reducing it. Participants became more likely to perceive caste discrimination where none was established and to endorse dehumanising descriptions of Brahmins.That’s not to say Indian-Americans cannot move the needle. They can when it exists within the ambit of the culture-war sphere, like getting Apu banned in The Simpsons, but in general, Indian-Americans struggle to counter global Anglosphere narratives about India, and that tends to pass the burden of Indian politics onto the diaspora.Great Power, No VoiceAnd this predicament is rather curious because Indian-Americans have never had greater representation in the US establishment, but with greater power didn’t come a greater voice.We’ve come a long way from the Samosa Caucus.New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, an Indian-American, is one of the most well-known Democratic faces across the country, but while he might shake a leg to the title track of Dhoom, he is still averse to referring to himself as Indian-American and even repeats mendacities about his ancestral state.Kash Patel might say Jai Shree Krishna at his FBI confirmation hearing but seldom speaks about atrocities against his co-religionists. Then again, he has been busy jet-setting across the country with his country-singer fiancée or chugging beer with hockey players.Vivek Ramaswamy, who was co-head of DOGE – before his abrupt exit following an epic diatribe on American laziness – is hoping to become governor of Ohio. While he was vocal about being Hindu during the presidential election debates – albeit presenting his version of Hinduism as crypto-Catholicism – he has been quieter in the run-up to the Ohio governor race. After the temple attack in Chicago, Ramaswamy’s silence was louder than his campaign’s obnoxious video attacking his opponent, Amy Acton.Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are seeking re-election to Congress. In California, Khanna faces fellow Indian-American Ritesh Tandon, while in Washington, Jayapal is being challenged by another Indian-American Republican, Nirav Sheth. Elsewhere, Amish Shah is contesting Arizona's 1st Congressional District, and Pooja Sethi is attempting to become the first Indian-American elected to the Texas Legislature.Yet, while Indian-Americans have become more prominent, none of the issues that affect the Indian community are particularly at the forefront. Racism against Indians is hardly worth discussing in American media outlets, and when it is, it is bundled together as discrimination against South Asians, which is often mentioned alongside Islamophobia.While there are numerous groups that now speak exclusively for the problems faced by Hindu-Americans, some of them, as Voltaire showed with the Holy Roman Empire, barely make a peep for actual Hindu issues – like the atrocities faced by minority Hindus in Bangladesh – but are more willing to hold forth on the Middle East.While MAGA, as Malcolm X famously described white conservatives’ reaction to black people, is fairly open about its animus towards Indians, claiming without proof that they participate in nepotism or H-1B fraud, the other side of the aisle is filled with people who often paint Indian-Americans as oppressors at the top of the caste hierarchy.While MAGA goes bonkers about a Hanuman statue on private land in Texas, its liberal opponents use the BAPS case in France to claim parochialism and misogyny among Hindu groups, even though a probe confirmed that the group had never explicitly asked for women to be removed from the Eiffel Tower.Neither of these issues directly affects the midterm results, but they show how easy it is to make Hindus or Indian-Americans pantomime villains.For a long time, Indian-Americans have been held up as a “model minority”, and perhaps that’s because they were never particularly bothered about political power, thinking that their status and money could protect them from the racism aimed at other minority groups. Or perhaps it was for that reason that Indian-Americans now find themselves at a crossroad. The numbers suggest Indian-Americans aren’t confused about whom they are going to vote for, even if they remain less certain about whom to identify with.Dem Vote, No Dem LoveAccording to the Carnegie Endowment's Indian American Attitudes Survey, released on November 2, 62% of Indian-American citizens intend to vote for Democratic candidates in the House elections, compared with just 19% for Republicans. Another 12% remain undecided. In Senate contests, the Democrats enjoy a similarly commanding lead of 63% to 21%.That's a 43-percentage-point Democratic advantage in House voting intentions, a rather remarkable figure considering the gains Trump appeared to make among Indian-Americans in 2024, when 30% supported him against 62% for Kamala Harris.But look beyond the surface and the numbers get more interesting.Despite the overwhelming preference for Democratic candidates, only 46% of Indian-American adults identify as Democrats, compared with 19% who identify as Republicans and 26% as independents. And those numbers have barely changed since January 2026.The most revealing finding, however, is that 35% of Indian-Americans intending to vote Democratic say they are doing so primarily because they oppose the Republican candidate or party, rather than because they support the Democrats. Among intending Republican voters, just 17% cite opposition to the Democrats as their principal motivation.So, while MAGA appears to have succeeded in alienating Indian-Americans as it has most other groups who flipped in 2024, it hasn't necessarily made them fall in love with the Democrats. A substantial section of the community is voting against the Republicans rather than enthusiastically embracing the alternative.The Democrats can count on their votes, but whether they can count on their affection is an entirely different matter. And perhaps the most peculiar aspect of this entire debate is how little the priorities of ordinary Indian-Americans resemble the ideological arguments conducted on their behalf.Carnegie's earlier 2026 survey found that inflation and prices were the biggest concern for 21% of respondents, followed by jobs and the economy at 17%, healthcare at 13% and immigration at 11%. Just 2% named US-India relations as their most important political issue.For all the American commentariat's fascination with caste, Hindu nationalism and the geopolitical implications of Indian identity, the average Indian-American appears rather more interested in the cost of living, employment and healthcare.Which raises an uncomfortable question for both parties.If a community can produce some of the richest people in America, occupy positions at the highest levels of government, finance political campaigns and remain one of the Democrats' most reliable voting constituencies, why does it still struggle to have its particular concerns heard?Perhaps that is the real political predicament facing Indian-Americans as they head to the polls. They may have acquired enough influence to help decide who governs America, but they still appear to be struggling to influence how America understands them. They know whom they intend to vote against. Who will speak for them after the votes are counted remains a rather more complicated question.About 133 years ago, a man born Narendranath Dutta said he was from India (rather than a princely state or presidency, as was the norm then) and preached tolerance at the World’s Parliament of Religions in a speech that evokes awe even today. It’s sad that, so many years later, Americans of all stripes have become particularly intolerant towards his descendants.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.summary: Supermarkets have reported problems from Estonia and Sweden to Portugal and Italy and many retainers have been forced to discard food.
articles.body:
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.

Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).

No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.

The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.

The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.

Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."

"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."

In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.

At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.

Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".

Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.

UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers

Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."

In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.

A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.

There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.

In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".

Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.

In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.

In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.

The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.

Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.

"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."

Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title: Hunt on for 'exceptional' new manager of Cornwall's Looe Island
articles.summary: The new manager will start each workday surrounded by nature at the island wildlife reserve.
articles.body:
The hunt is on for a new manager to care for a wildlife reserve on a Cornish island.

Cornwall Wildlife Trust said it was is recruiting for the post on Looe Island in the Whitsand and Looe Bay Marine Conservation Area.

Visitors are only allowed in organised trips and the island has Cornwall's largest breeding colony of the great black-backed gull, as well as being home to grey seals.

The trust said it was looking for an "exceptional" person and the job, with an application closing date of Sunday 15 November, offered "an opportunity to combine your passion for conservation with practical leadership, people management and a flair for creating a truly special visitor experience".

Accommodation was provided for the manager and the role included caring for wildlife, leading a team of volunteers and welcoming visitors, the trust added.

Looe Island was given to the wildlife trust in 2004 by sisters Babs and Evelyn Atkins, who lived there and wrote two books about island life.

It was also known as St George's Island during World War Two.

It sits one mile (1.6km) off Looe and covers just over 22 acres (8.9 hectares) , including woodland, grassland, shingle and a rocky reef teaming with wildlife.

The trust said: "The island is a sensitive habitat and provides important sanctuary for marine life, seabirds and other coastal species. Nesting birds include cormorants, shags and oystercatchers.

"There are a mix of habitats which, in such a small space, means it provides a really important space for wildlife."

articles.title: Iran commander sets out five conditions for regional security
articles.summary: Mediator Qatar says US and Iran are studying proposals to resume negotiations and that it was ‘hopeful’ of an agreement.
articles.body:
The chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces has laid out five conditions for what he calls a roadmap to lasting security, as Qatar said it was “hopeful” that Tehran and Washington could reach a deal paving the way for future negotiations, despite overnight US strikes on Qeshm Island .

Major-General Ali Abdollahi’s plan calls for an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon and the Gaza Strip, the complete lifting of sanctions and the unfreezing of Iranian assets and war reparations, Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported on Tuesday.

The plan also calls for recognition of Iran’s sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, and a guarantee against future aggression under a regional security framework for West Asia.

The plan comes as Qatar steps up mediation efforts amid fears the US-Israel war on Iran, launched in late February, could escalate after the midterm elections in the United States on Tuesday.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Majed al-Ansari said in his weekly briefing in Doha on Tuesday that a Qatari delegation held a meeting with Iranian officials in Tehran for more than three hours on Monday, before returning to Doha that evening. Both sides are now reviewing Qatar’s proposal, he said, with mediators exchanging proposals between them in real time.

“If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations,” al-Ansari said, adding that Qatar would not speculate on whether an agreement or a military escalation was more likely.

He warned that any escalation, whether attacks on Iranian territory or on shipping, “will have an impact on the negotiations”, and said continuing the Qatari-Pakistani mediation remained a priority. He reiterated that freedom of navigation in Hormuz was nonnegotiable, referring to Doha’s condemnation of the targeting of the Qatari tanker Al-Mayda.

Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas said mediators were aiming to avert a new round of fighting.

He said a Qatari delegation visited Iran on Friday in response to a letter to Iran from US Vice President JD Vance, and an Iranian delegation travelled to Qatar the following day.

“The Qataris are trying to mediate with Iran, not on a peace deal, but on a framework to restart the negotiations,” he said. Of Monday’s brief visit, he added: “The reading is that the Qataris carried a message to Tehran and immediately left after that.”

“The main issue is the mistrust between the two parties,” Atas said. “The Iranians say that twice previously the US attacked them when they were engaged in diplomacy. That’s why they’re asking for concrete steps, such as lifting sanctions, removing the naval blockade, returning frozen Iranian assets and letting Iran sell oil on the global market.”

US officials reportedly said the military carried out limited strikes on Qeshm Island on Monday that did not amount to a resumption of major combat operations, saying Iran had tried to target a US aircraft and the attack took out the launcher.

One official called it “a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets”. IRNA reported five explosions on the island, with more blasts heard in Bandar Lengeh. President Donald Trump had said on October 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday it downed two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm and destroyed an MQ-9 drone east of the strait.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s lead negotiator, said, “The ball is in America’s court to prevent war.”

Tehran’s Hamshahri newspaper reported that Iran had updated its target bank to include US bases and infrastructure in Europe.

On Tuesday, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on X that Washington’s response to Iran’s demands needs to be explicit and convincing.

“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing,” he said.

Rezaei added that the United States’ response “must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them; only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened”.

Zeidon Alkinani, the founding director of the Arab Perceptions Institute, said both sides remained open to diplomacy.

“ Diplomacy and force are running in parallel,” Alkinani told Al Jazeera. “The diplomatic channel is alive – it has always been since March, but there hasn’t unfortunately been a fundamental breakthrough.”

Vance had said on Monday he was optimistic about reaching a negotiated settlement.

However, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday Iran was neither waiting for the outcome of US midterm elections nor shaping its policies around them.

articles.body: GUWAHATI: As many as 43 students of Assam Engineering College (AEC) in Guwahati fell ill after consuming contaminated water and food prepared using it, following the death of a monkey in a hostel water tank on the college campus.The monkey reportedly drowned in the tank, contaminating the water supply used by students. articles.title: Very cold war: Who’s attacking Europe’s supermarket freezers?
articles.summary: Cold stores in supermarkets across Europe have been targeted in a cyberattack with no clear culprit.
articles.body:
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe have been targeted by a cyberattack that raised the temperature of internet-linked units, destroying and damaging large quantities of food.

On Monday, fridges and freezers at more than 100 shops in several European countries ran hot. Cyberattacks on supermarkets began last month, when hundreds of French supermarkets were left with spoiled food and damage to units which had overheated, costing millions of euros.

So far, it remains unclear why hackers targeted the supermarkets, but attacks have spread across the continent and even to the United States.

Which countries in Europe have been targeted?

On Monday, several supermarkets in Europe were affected, including the following:

Dutch supermarket operator Delhaize said dozens of its shops in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit by an “IT incident”.

French retailer Carrefour said about 15 of its 700 Belgian locations were hit by refrigeration problems.

The Colruyt group, which runs Spar stores in Belgium as franchises, said five of its shops were affected.

Swedish Coop said cooling systems at seven of its 800 stores were affected, with disruptions ranging from complete shutdowns to partial operation.

Swedish furniture retailer IKEA, which also operates restaurants at its stores, said one site in Mons, Belgium, had been affected by a cyberattack.

De Laet & Van Haver, the Belgian butchery chain, said the temperature in its fridges at its store in Hove, south of Antwerp, was raised as high as 18 degrees Celsius, ruining meat worth about 15,000 euros ($16,764).

The food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber-incident affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores in Ireland.

In October, hundreds of French supermarkets suffered cyberattacks , spoiling tonnes of food, causing fires and melting parts of refrigeration units.

In August, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, went into defrost mode, spoiling all the frozen food they contained, according to a post on Facebook by the base.

The same month, the naval station in Newport, Rhode Island, reported on Facebook that its refrigeration system was affected, leaving only dry goods were available for purchase.

The Pentagon considered the freezer malfunctions on the military bases to be a suspected hack, the Reuters news agency reported late last month, citing four officials close to the matter.

One official said Pentagon investigators were communicating with the French authorities about the issue.

How are cyberattackers targeting fridges and freezers?

Hackers can access the controls of fridges and freezers which use internet software and raise their temperature in order to spoil frozen food.

In some cases, hackers have increased the temperature of appliances to as high as 50C (122F) in European supermarkets, causing them to melt or even catch fire.

Awais Rashid, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Bristol in the UK, explained that many supermarket refrigeration systems which are remotely managed and, often by third parties, have not been given necessary software updates to prevent hackers.

“In line with established cyber security practices, these systems should be managed via secure networks. However, this is not the case in these incidents and they are accessible on the Internet,” Rashid told Al Jazeera.

“A remote managing party can access a web server on the controller to configure the system including temperature changes and maintenance. There are known vulnerabilities in several controllers (many of which are past their end of life),” he said.

Rashid added that vulnerabilities include “easily guessable” passwords, which would mean anyone could gain access.

The motive behind the attacks is unclear, but authorities believe it may be a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supplies.

On Monday, the European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, Christophe Hansen, said the attacks on fridges were a “deliberate attempt to disrupt” the bloc’s food supply and to undermine consumer confidence.

He added that while “food security is not currently at risk … the food waste and impact on businesses are real”.

Rashid said that while there are few details about who may be behind the attacks or what their motives are, it is likely that these are “the motive here is likely disruption”.

“This has financial impacts on the supermarkets but also societal impacts in terms of security of the food supply chain. Critically, this risks undermining trust in infrastructures on which people rely daily,” he said.

On Monday, Belgium’s prosecutor’s office announced that it had opened a criminal investigation into the latest fridge cyberattacks. But so far, no one has taken responsibility.

Theories have emerged linking state actors to cyberattacks generally, with North Korea most recently accused of being behind last week’s $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency heist, which forced the crypto group to freeze accounts.

European intelligence officials have also warned that Russia is escalating its shadow war on the continent amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine, with cyberattacks among the methods it uses.

On Tuesday, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that Britain needs to be prepared for an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyberattack on its critical national infrastructure within the next two years.

“By 2028, it is highly likely that Russia, China and other nation states will routinely use AI-cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals, with the UK facing an increase in scale and speed of sophisticated cyberattacks,” the NCSC said in a report.

The report comes shortly after the UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign, calling on citizens to stockpile enough tinned food, bottled water and cash to last three days in the event of a cyberattack or national emergency.

Rashid said that as our infrastructure becomes increasingly digitised, the risk of disruption from cyberattacks, especially “cyber-physical infrastructures such as refrigeration systems”, has risen.

“However, we should also note that a lot of our digital infrastructures operate safely everyday because good security practices enable that. The world works because cyber security works effectively. So it is important that all businesses follow good cyber security practices,” he said.

articles.title: Two Washington sisters sued over fence lines on both sides of their home after a survey exposed a boundary dispute; the courts backed their neighbours, ordered one fence removed and upheld legal-fee awards
articles.summary: Two sisters in Washington, US, who went to court over fences separating their home from neighbouring properties have lost their appeal after judges upheld
articles.body: Two sisters in Washington, US, who went to court over fences separating their home from neighbouring properties have lost their appeal after judges upheld rulings in favour of both neighbours.Emily and Helene Hofbauer had challenged property boundaries in Kennewick following a survey that showed the fences did not match the official boundary lines. On July 21, the Washington Court of Appeals upheld an order requiring them to remove a fence encroaching on one neighbour's land. It also upheld legal-fee awards to both neighbours and granted them additional legal fees for the appeal.According to the ruling, the dispute began after the sisters bought their home in 2019. Their property stood between two other houses, with Kevin Dement living to the west and Jessica Horst to the east. Fences separated the three properties, but questions about their positions eventually led the sisters to commission a survey.The survey, completed in October 2023, found that both fences stood a few feet west of the legally recorded property boundaries. This meant the western fence extended onto Dement's land, while the eastern fence stood inside the sisters' property.In January 2024, the sisters filed a lawsuit naming both neighbours. They claimed rights over the strip of land beside Dement's property, arguing that they and previous owners had used it openly and continuously for years. The case also brought Horst's fence into question, although the original complaint did not clearly explain what action the sisters wanted against her.How the two neighbours respondedDement rejected the sisters' claim and asked the court to order the removal of the fence from his property. Horst took a different position. She acknowledged that her fence extended onto the sisters' land but argued that she had acquired ownership rights over the enclosed strip because the fence had been there since 2007.Both neighbours relied on a legal principle known as adverse possession. Under Washington law, a person may claim ownership of another person's land after possessing it openly, exclusively and continuously under certain conditions for at least 10 years.Horst argued that she had met those requirements. The sisters admitted they could not produce evidence to challenge her claim, and the trial court ruled in her favour. It recognised her ownership of the disputed eastern strip and dismissed the sisters' claim against her.The dispute with Dement continued. Before trial, the sisters withdrew their claim to his land after the court excluded their expert witness. However, Dement's request for removal of the fence remained unresolved, so the case proceeded.Conflicting statements about western fenceDuring the trial, Dement said an old, damaged fence had separated the properties before either side bought their homes. According to him, the sisters replaced it after moving in. He could not say whether the new fence followed exactly the same line as the previous one.Helene gave a different account. She said the old fence had been repaired and rebuilt rather than removed. She also told the court that she did not know whether it extended onto Dement's property.That statement became important because it differed from what she had said earlier. In a sworn declaration filed in December 2024, Helene had acknowledged that the survey placed the fence between 1.83 and 4.06 feet west of the recorded boundary.Emily also testified that she initially believed the fence marked the correct boundary because of information provided by the estate agent. She later learnt that it was not on the legal property line.The trial court concluded that the fence stood on Dement's land and ordered the sisters to remove it. It also rejected Helene's attempt to take a position inconsistent with her earlier court statements.Why appeals court upheld orderThe sisters challenged the decision, arguing that the trial court had not properly considered whether removing the fence would cause unnecessary hardship.Washington law allows courts to make exceptions in certain circumstances rather than automatically ordering an encroaching structure to be removed. However, the person seeking an exception must provide convincing evidence supporting it.The appeals court found that the sisters had not done so. They had provided no evidence of the cost of removing or relocating the fence, or of the value of Dement's land affected by it. The judges also rejected their argument that the trial court had improperly relied on a survey that was not admitted as evidence.Sisters also lose challenge to legal feesThe sisters separately challenged the legal fees awarded to both neighbours. They argued that Horst should not receive fees because their original complaint had not clearly made a claim against her. They also maintained that Dement should not qualify for fees because they had voluntarily withdrawn their claim before trial.The appeals court rejected both arguments. It found that Horst had successfully defended herself and won her ownership claim. Dement was also treated as the successful party after the sisters withdrew their claim against him.The judges found that the lower court had properly examined the legal bills and assessed whether the amounts were reasonable. The ruling did not specify the final dollar amounts of the awards.The appeals court therefore left the earlier decisions unchanged and granted Horst and Dement reasonable legal fees for defending the appeal.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel’s opposition leaders back Eisenkot to oust Netanyahu
articles.summary: Opposition promises to form a government quickly but remains split over whether to ally with Arab-led parties.
articles.body:
Israel’s opposition leaders have agreed to back former military chief Gadi Eisenkot as prime minister, promising to replace Benjamin Netanyahu’s government as quickly as possible.

The five party heads met on Tuesday in the city of Herzliya, north of Tel Aviv, in their first joint meeting since the October 27 election , which left neither bloc with a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

The agreement comes a day before President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with parties on who should form the next government.

But the bloc remains divided over whether to ally with Arab-led parties, whose support could prove decisive.

In a joint statement, the leaders said all their parties would recommend Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, to Herzog, and that negotiating teams would immediately begin drafting policy guidelines and coalition agreements.

“The party leaders are coordinated and will act immediately to replace the ‘Oct. 7 government’ with a national emergency government,” the statement said.

The meeting brought together Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman, Yair Golan of the Democrats, and Yair Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party, according to The Jerusalem Post.

The leaders stood by four principles set out by Eisenkot, including that all parties in government recognise Israel as a Jewish state and label Hamas a terrorist group, conditions that could exclude some Arab-led parties.

“We don’t have time – we must act with great urgency,” Bennett, whose party came third, told reporters.

Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, the opposition 48, and Arab-led parties 19, with the Joint List taking 11 and Ra’am eight. A majority requires 61 seats.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the largest Arab-led party in the next parliament, said the opposition needed to accept “political reality” and join forces to remove Netanyahu.

Golan is the only opposition leader openly backing an alliance with Arab-led parties, saying it is racist to exclude them.

He met the leaders of Arab-led parties before the talks and promised to tackle high crime faced by Palestinian citizens of Israel in their communities.

Afterwards, the two sides stressed their “shared interest in using the parliamentary majority to bring down the Netanyahu-Ben-Gvir-Smotrich government and replace it”, according to a statement.

Liberman has firmly opposed including Arab-led parties, although he also wants to avoid another election.

Israel’s minority Arab population has long been marginalised in politics, and even more so since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7 and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

At least two former Palestinian politicians and one current member of the Knesset have been arrested briefly for comments or acts deemed critical of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

Arab citizens of Israel are descendants of Palestinians who managed to remain within the borders of the newly established Israeli state in 1948 after the Nakba , or catastrophe. They make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population.

On Monday, Netanyahu called for a “broad national government” under his leadership, saying his Likud party, with 27 seats, remained the largest. No opposition leader has expressed openness to joining him.

He has ruled out a coalition with Arab-majority lists, alleging they “support terrorism and deny the existence of the Jewish state”.

Netanyahu, 76, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, is on trial on corruption charges and is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in the enclave since Israel began its war in October 2023.

Herzog will hold consultations on Wednesday and Thursday. Eisenkot could receive the most recommendations if he secures the backing of Arab lawmakers.

articles.title: Rio Tinto joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
articles.summary: Rio Tinto is jointly funding a A$28m "toad containment zoe" to protect the Pilbara region.
articles.body:
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.

The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.

While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.

Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.

The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.

Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.

"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."

The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.

In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.

If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.

The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.

A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.

The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.

Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.

There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.

Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.

He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

articles.body: The Dartmoor home of former Conservative MP Ann Widdecombe, who was murdered in July 2026, has gone on the market for £900,000, just four months after her death. The five-bedroom property in Haytor Vale, Devon, where she was found dead following a hammer attack, is being marketed by estate agents Knight Frank under its original name, Thurlecot.The property, which Widdecombe had renamed ‘Widdecombe’s Rest’ after moving there following her retirement from Parliament, comes with five reception rooms, three bathrooms, a swimming pool, stables and extensive gardens. The asking price represents a reported 50 per cent increase on the £600,000 she paid for the house in 2008.According to the property's listing on Rightmove, the detached bungalow spans approximately 5,139 square feet and is surrounded by gardens. Knight Frank describes it as being within easy walking distance of the open moor, with a south-facing position offering privacy and views of the surrounding countryside.Estate agents include special note about Ann Widdecombe’s deathThe circumstances surrounding Widdecombe's death have also been acknowledged in the property's sales brochure. As reported by The Daily Mail and The Sun, the estate agents have included a note under the property information section stating: "A significant event occurred at the property in 2026, involving the unlawful death of an occupant. Further details can be provided by the agent."The listing also showcases the house's spacious interiors, including a sitting room with a fireplace, a stylish fitted kitchen and a large library-cum-dining room. The property has a stone-paved terrace running along its front, which the agents say benefits from long-distance views of the surrounding countryside.Home was targeted by visitors after the murderThe property also attracted unwanted attention after the murder, with locals reportedly complaining that visitors were turning up to take selfies outside the crime scene or attempting to look through the windows.According to The Sun, large wooden gates were subsequently installed at the entrance and secured with a heavy chain and padlock. The sign bearing the name ‘Widdecombe’s Rest’ was also removed.A local resident told the publication that the incident had shocked the entire community, adding that Widdecombe was genuinely loved by villagers. Residents reportedly hoped the additional security measures would help restore normality in the neighbourhood.What happened to Ann Widdecombe?Widdecombe, 78, was found dead in the kitchen of her Dartmoor home on July 9, 2026, after failing to attend a scheduled online appearance on a Channel 5 programme the previous day.According to details presented in court, she had been eating lunch when she was allegedly attacked with a hammer on July 8. Prosecutors told the court that she had been struck 21 times on the head. Her gardener discovered her body during a welfare check after she could not be contacted.Joshua Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, has been charged with her murder and remanded in custody. He has also faced a separate charge relating to the preparation of a terrorist act. The allegations remain subject to court proceedings, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.From Parliament to Strictly Come DancingWiddecombe retired from the House of Commons in 2010 after representing the Conservative Party for more than two decades. She subsequently moved to Dartmoor, a region she had a personal connection with, and named her new home ‘Widdecombe’s Rest’.However, her departure from Parliament did not mean an end to her public appearances. She became a contestant on Strictly Come Dancing in 2010, where she was partnered with professional dancer Anton du Beke. articles.title: How US midterms have cost a record $12bn as cost of living soars
articles.summary: Candidates, donors and super PACs are spending more than ever on political campaigns.
articles.body:
The US midterm elections are on track to be the most expensive for candidates and political donors in history. According to OpenSecrets, a research group that tracks money in US politics, close to a record $12bn has been spent by candidates and outside political groups on campaigning.

The world’s richest man, Elon Musk alone has given $445 million to the Republicans, according to campaign finance records.

Critics have questioned the huge sums of money being spent to sway voting during an election cycle in which the cost of living and affordability have been the key issues in most campaign agendas.

They argue that campaign spending policy gives wealthy donors, corporations and special interest groups outsized influence over candidate and policy selection.

Why has so much been spent on these elections?

US elections are funded in two ways. Firstly, candidates can directly raise money for their campaigns. In the lead-up to these midterms, Democratic candidates are expected to have spent more than $2.2bn compared with $1.4bn by Republican candidates, according to OpenSecrets.

Secondly, corporations, unions and other associations can spend money on election campaigns, independently of individual candidates’ campaigns, in a process known as “outside spending”.

Previously, these organisations were barred from funding adverts close to elections in order to prevent corruption or the appearance of corruption. But in 2010, the US Supreme Court overturned that rule, treating election communications as protected political speech.

In a related ruling, a lower court struck down limits on the size of contributions these groups could raise, provided they did not coordinate directly with candidates.

Since then, Federal Election Commission disclosure data shows such spending on elections has increased hugely, nearly tripling in the past decade alone from $4.12bn in 2016 to an estimated $11.9bn for 2026’s midterm elections.

This “outside spending” is largely driven by groups called independent expenditure-only political action committees – better known as super PACs – which organise the funding and then spend it on advertising or other initiatives in support of candidates or parties.

There are no limits on the amount of money donors can give to outside spending groups such as super PACs.

That has been the case since the Supreme Court ruled that unlimited contributions to groups which do not coordinate directly with candidates are protected under free speech laws.

The majority of super PACs are politically aligned and organised in line with either the Democratic or Republican Party.

Among the largest super PACs are the Senate Leadership Fund, which has spent $489 million, and MAGA Inc, with $353 million, both for Republican candidates. The Senate Majority PAC and the House Majority PAC have spent $248 million and $192 million respectively on Democratic candidates.

Other super PACs are organised by individuals and special interest groups, such as the Republican-supporting America PAC founded and funded by Elon Musk and the Democracy PAC funded and organised by George Soros which backs Democratic candidates.

Super PACs report on their direct contributors as well as financial activity to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) every month during election years, and every six months during non-election years. But contributors may include organisations whose own funding sources are not publicly disclosed.

This means that funds can pass through multiple organisations – sometimes through other PACs, known as “shell PACs” – before they are spent on campaign-related activities or advertising, making it difficult to trace contributions back to their original source.

When an original source of political spending cannot be identified, the funds are commonly described as “dark money”. According to OpenSecrets, “dark money” contributions will surpass a record $1.5bn in these midterm elections. That is up from the previous record of $1.35bn set in 2024 and has prompted concerns about the transparency of funding for political candidates.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accused the nonprofit lobbying group, American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), of spending “millions in dark money”, for example, on pro-Israel candidates.

Public records reviewed by Al Jazeera found that AIPAC has channelled millions of dollars through shell PACs ahead of the US midterm elections.

AIPAC is one of the best-known super PACs and has attracted criticism in recent years, particularly in light of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The lobbying group decided to end endorsements and direct campaign contributions after a challenging year.

AIPAC was founded as the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs by American journalist and lawyer Isaiah Kenan in the 1950s. It was renamed American Israel Public Affairs Committee in 1959 and has grown to more than 6 million members. On its website it says “AIPAC helps pro-Israel candidates no matter their race, religion or background, and opposes anti-Israel candidates no matter their race, religion or background”.

Much of the money AIPAC spends has been channelled through the United Democracy Project (UDP), another registered super PAC affiliated with it. AIPAC has spent money on both Republican and Democratic campaigns, and has been accused of using money raised by Republican donors to fund adverts for “moderate” Democratic candidates in the hope of unseating or blocking progressive candidates, particularly those with pro-Palestine views.

That includes nearly $15 million spent on advertising and campaigning for pro-Israel Democrat George Latimer to stand against progressive Jamaal Bowman in New York’s 16th congressional district Democratic House primary in June 2024. Latimer ultimately won that vote.

AIPAC also spent $5.24 million on advertising for Wesley Bell against Cori Bush, who has criticised Israel’s war on Gaza, in the St Louis, Missouri primary which Bush lost. UDP has also spent $20.7 million to campaign against Abdul El Sayed in the Michigan Senate race.

Reject AIPAC , a coalition of progressive advocacy groups, launched a campaign calling on candidates for federal office to promise not to take endorsements or contributions from AIPAC or aligned PACs in 2024.

The coalition includes Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party, as well as organisations focused on Palestinian rights, including the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights Action, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP) Action and the IfNotNow Movement.

The greatest amounts of money have been spent in “toss-up” states – where candidates face a close race – including Georgia, Texas and Michigan, which has seen record spending in its Senate contest between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

In Michigan, an estimated $333m has been spent on the campaign. Rogers has raised about $23m in direct contributions, while El-Sayed has brought in approximately $54m. Outside groups, however, have spent about $169m supporting Rogers and roughly $94m supporting El-Sayed.

But multiple polls have shown that the cost of living and the economy are the key current concerns for both Republican and Democratic voters.

This spending comes as the US is in the grip of a cost-of-living crisis, with fuel prices in particular soaring as a result of the Trump administration’s war on Iran. Prices have skyrocketed since February after shipping disruption in the Strait of Hormuz caused the cost of diesel to spike by 65 percent and fertiliser costs rose by up to 40 percent causing food prices to rise.

El Sayed, in particular, has campaigned on reforming election funding and taking “money out of politics”.

But a football fan on X responded: “$12 billion in political ads for the midterms, amaze me. Spending that much in such a useless way while saying we don’t have money for schools and/or healthcare.”

According to the Iran War Energy Cost Tracker, Americans have spent at least $150bn on petrol and diesel since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, 30 percent more than they would have spent without the war raising prices. $12bn could cover 8 percent of those fuel costs or roughly $92 per household.

The Trump administration included $12bn in spending cuts for the Department of Education as part of the 2026 fiscal budget. That $12bn could pay for roughly 1 percent of the federal government budget for public schools.

There have also been spending cuts in medical and science research funding, including to the National Institutes of Health (NIH). $12bn could increase the NIH research funding budget of $47bn by one-quarter.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Hardeep Puri is set to win the upcoming Rajya Sabha bypoll unopposed from Madhya Pradesh after the nomination papers filed by
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Hardeep Puri is set to win the upcoming Rajya Sabha bypoll unopposed from Madhya Pradesh after the nomination papers filed by two candidates were rejected by the returning officer.According to news agency PTI, the nominations of Congress-backed candidates Rajkumar Lohani and Kante Sayanna were rejected on the last day of scrutiny.Meanwhile, the two independent candidates, along with Congress leader Hemant Katare, also objected to Puri's nomination papers, contending that his affidavit in Form 26 was invalid and incomplete.However, returning officer Umesh Sharma examined the objections and held that Puri had not violated any requirements of the Representation of the People Act."No defect was found in Puri's papers," the returning officer said in his order.Congress termed the order an "attack on Indian democracy" and said it would move court against it."This is an attack on Indian democracy. Despite such significant errors, the nomination was not rejected," Katare and Congress MLA Atif Aqeel said in a statement.The bypoll was necessitated by the resignation of former Union minister L Murugan, who vacated the seat on October 14. His term in the Rajya Sabha was originally scheduled to end on April 2, 2030.The Election Commission announced the schedule for the bypoll on October 22.According to the schedule, the notification for the election will be issued on October 26. The last date for filing nominations is November 2, while scrutiny will take place on November 3. articles.title: BJP worker seeks advocate general’s consent to initiate criminal action for contempt of court against CJP’s Saurav Das
articles.summary: BJP worker Vivekanand Gupta seeks advocate general’s consent to file criminal contempt case against CJP’s Saurav Das over judiciary-critical X post.
articles.body: Mumbai: BJP party worker Vivekanand Gupta has filed an application with the advocate general seeking consent to initiate criminal action for contempt of court against Saurav Das of the Cockroach Janata Party.Referring to Das’ post on social media, Gupta said he has scandalised the judiciary by alleging that judges decide cases on “personal biases and myths” instead of the rules of law, and by calling the judiciary “a big black blot on our country.”On Nov 3, Das had posted: “Remember that we have judges who would much rather preach and judge based on personal biases and myths than strictly go by the rule of law and keep a check on arbitrary, excessive, colourable use of power by the state. It’s a big black blot on our country and those in contempt of Constitution will pay for it.”Gupta, in his application, stated that the post on X appears to have been published in connection with the Bombay High Court hearing related to Imran Khan versus State of Maharashtra where Khan had been issued a notice by the state to leave India for his part in the SIR agitation in Mumbai.
